Love Is Strong as Death
LUV iz STRAWNG az DETH
n. phr. (the Song's great declaration on the strength of covenant love)
Hebrew azzah ka-mavet ahabah — az, strong, fierce, unyielding; mavet, death; ahabah, love; the comparison is not of sweetness but of grip, death being the one power nothing escapes.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

“Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.” The comparison the Song chooses is startling and deliberate. Death is not praised for beauty; it is feared for its hold — it takes what it takes and does not give back. Love, says the bride, has that kind of grip. Three further strokes fill out the figure. The seal is a mark of ownership pressed into wax or worn on the hand, so the request is to be owned and openly claimed. Jealousy here is not the vice but the rightful fierceness of exclusive covenant love, the same word Scripture uses of God's own jealousy for His people. And the coals name its burning: a flame that the Hebrew ties to the LORD's own name. The Song is Solomon's, the canonical celebration of marriage between one man and one woman, and the Reformed have always read it at two levels without confusing them — the literal marriage it plainly describes and commends, and the covenant love of Christ for His church which marriage was made to picture. On either level the sentence stands: this love holds like the grave, and the apostle says that nothing shall separate us from it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Strong, having physical active power; firm; not easily broken or subdued. Love, an affection of the mind excited by beauty and worth. Love is strong as death, Song of Solomon 8:6, the unyielding grip of covenant love.

Strong, having active power or force; firm; not easily broken or overcome.

Love, an affection of the mind excited by beauty, worth, or kindness.

Hebrew az, strong, fierce, unyielding; said of lions and of hard things.

Hebrew qin'ah, jealousy or zeal; used of God's own jealousy for His people.

Hebrew chotham, a seal, the mark of ownership pressed or worn.

Key Scripture

Son 8:6 — "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame."

Son 8:7 — "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned."

Rom 8:38 — "For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come,"

Joh 15:13 — "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends."

Modern Corruption

The verse is lifted into wedding sentiment with the jealousy and the exclusiveness cut out, and from the other side the Song is reduced to an anthology of unconnected poems with no Solomonic voice and no covenant doctrine.

expand to see more

Engraved on rings and read at weddings, the sentence is now chiefly heard as a compliment to romantic feeling — and the two clauses that make it bite are regularly omitted. The bride asks to be sealed, which is to be owned, and she names jealousy as cruel as the grave, which is the fierce exclusiveness of a covenant that admits no third party. A love strong as death is by definition a love that cannot be shared out or renegotiated, so the verse is the enemy of every arrangement that keeps marriage provisional. Preached whole, it commends what our age will not have: permanence, possession, and a jealousy that is a virtue.

The critical treatment errs in the other direction, dissolving the Song into a collection of unrelated love lyrics gathered late and bearing no single authorial voice, which conveniently removes both its Solomonic attribution and any covenant theology in it. The book names its author in its first verse, the canon has received it as Solomon's, and its movement from courtship to consummation to this closing seal is coherent. The principle to recover is the one the Reformed have held: the Song is literally about marriage and typically about Christ and His church, and a reading that denies either its unity or its Author leaves the church without the only book of Scripture given wholly to the love of husband and wife.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew az, fierce and unyielding; mavet, death; qin'ah, covenant jealousy; shalhebetyah, a flame whose ending is the divine name — strength of grip, not sweetness, is the comparison.

expand to see more

Hebrew az, strong, fierce, unyielding — the grip of a thing, not its sweetness.

Hebrew mavet, death, chosen because nothing escapes its hold.

Hebrew qin'ah, jealousy or zeal, the rightful fierceness of exclusive love.

Hebrew chotham, a seal, worn on hand or heart as the mark of ownership.

Hebrew shalhebetyah, a vehement flame, ending in the shortened divine name.
